name: Liam Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm studying software engineering, so a normal week is lectures from nine, a coding lab on Tuesdays, and a lot of evenings on my laptop. I live in a student house with four people, and I run a small business selling refurbished phones on the side, which brings in around 200 a month. My dad runs a trucking firm with eleven trucks, my mum is a school secretary, and they cover about half of what I need. On Sundays I volunteer at our church's youth football club and I coach the under-tens. I use AI tools every day, for code, for writing my sales listings, even for planning my week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's probably fair. At my uni, I'd tell people it's useful but not magic, so don't build your life on it. In my business I'd say it still saves me a couple of hours a week writing listings, and that's enough for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm okay with that. My degree stays valuable, and I'm already ahead on the tools. My real concern is Dad's trucking firm, because fuel and insurance costs keep eating his margin, and plateau or not, that doesn't change. If he loses a contract, my parents' help to me stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going: study, keep selling phones, and coach on Sundays. I'd try to raise the phone business to 400 a month, by finding a second supplier. I'd ask Dad if I could help him with his route planning over the summer, since it's a good practical project, and I'd apply for a paid internship.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm for myself, and a bit watchful about Dad's firm. Nothing I can't handle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you grow the phone business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd find a second wholesaler and try a new product, like refurbished tablets. I'd test it with ten units first. Last month I lost about 60 on a batch of bad screens, so I'm more careful now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did that batch teach you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That cheap isn't always cheap. I wrote the bad batch off as the cost of learning, and I now check every unit before I list it. It's boring, but it means fewer returns.

In my business it still saves me a couple of hours a week writing listings.
think: I'm **okay with that**: my degree stays valuable and I'm ahead on the tools.
The real concern is **Dad's trucking firm**, where fuel and insurance eat margin.

Find a **second supplier** and aim for 400 a month.
Help Dad with **route planning** over the summer and apply for a paid internship.
feel: **Calm** for myself, and a bit watchful about Dad's firm.

fieldNote: Treats the plateau as **fine** for him; the trucking firm's costs are his real worry.

Help Dad plan his truck routes over the summer
Keep coaching the under-tens on Sundays

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's an opportunity, for people who learn quickly, and a risk for people who don't. At church, I'd say we should be ready to help older folks who get left behind. Online, I'd probably talk about how small businesses can use the tools as well as big firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm excited and a bit cautious. I know junior programmers are exposed, but I'm adaptive and I like risk. I'd rather be the one who builds with the tools than the one who gets replaced by them. Still, I'd be lying if I said it didn't give me a knot sometimes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on the tools, and build some proper projects that go beyond coursework. I'd pitch my dad on a dispatch assistant for his firm, one that plans routes and handles customer messages. If it works, that's a reference, and it might become a product. I'd also put the profit from my phone sales into a small cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and uneasy. A bit like taking the first corner on a bike, a bit fast, but you're up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad say about the dispatch assistant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say, will it break? Then he'd say, how much? He's practical, he's seen gadgets come and go. But two of his dispatchers are retiring, so he might listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the firm would worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office staff, Sandra and Hamid, who do the paperwork and the phones. I'd want my dad's office staff to run the new system, not be replaced by it, because they know the customers. I think that's fairer, and it's also better business.

say: It's an **opportunity** for people who learn quickly, and a risk for people who don't.
At church I'd say we should help **older folks** who get left behind.

steps.text: Build a route and message assistant for Dad's firm
Use AI tools daily and build two projects
Put phone profits into a small cushion
Turn the dispatch tool into a product for other firms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's moving faster than anyone planned, and people should look after their families and their neighbours first. I'd say it at church, where the older folks would need reassurance. At uni I'd say we should demand honest plans from companies and government, not slogans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be scared. By 2028 I'd be in my second year, and my whole field changes before I graduate. Dad's trucks are hands-on, so they'd last till about 2031, but dispatch, billing and customer calls would go to software straight away. If the firm's margins fall, my parents' help to me stops, and so does the family's income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk with Dad about what to protect, and I'd stop spending on anything extra. I'd put more time into my business and into building real products with the tools, because I'd want income that doesn't depend on a job offer. I'd see if the university has hardship funds, and I'd offer to help Dad switch his firm to software that cuts its overhead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lose sleep over my parents' mortgage and the drivers' families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which drivers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big Ron and Dev have worked with my dad for eleven years. They're like uncles to me. If the trucks stop, those guys have kids. That's what I think about, more than my own degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave uni?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I could earn more building things, maybe. I'd rather finish, but I'd drop it if it meant my parents didn't lose the house. Family first.

say: It's moving faster than anyone planned, so look after **families and neighbours** first.
At uni I'd ask for **honest plans** from companies and government, not slogans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for people who start now. At church I'd tell the young ones to learn something useful and save a bit. At uni I'd say let's stop arguing about whether it's real and start building things that matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel anxious but ready. I'd graduate in 2029 or 2030 and the big change would come about a year later. I'd want to have something of my own by then: a business, a product, a customer base, anything that isn't just a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow my phone business and my software skills together. I'd do an internship each summer, ideally at a small company where I'd learn to run things. I'd help Dad modernise his firm, with routing, billing and customer messages, so it's lean before everyone else's. I'd save 4,000 by graduation, and maybe move some of it into an index fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a bit of fight in it. I'd rather be busy than just worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your dad to do in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get the firm ready to either stand on its own with fewer staff, or sell at a decent price before things get hard. I'd show him the numbers. He'd resist at first, but he can see a spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you build a business from this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. If trucking firms all have the same problems with dispatch and paperwork, a tool that fixes them might sell. I'd test it on Dad's firm and two others, and see if they pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time, and people shouldn't be afraid. At church I'd say the young should learn skills, the old should share what they know, and we should look after each other. At uni I'd say build something and don't wait to be asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be calm. I'd be 28, hopefully with a company and some savings. The thing I'd worry about is my dad. He'd be in his sixties with a trucking firm that might not survive the robots in 2039, and he's not the type who'd retire easily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, work for a company to learn the craft, and run my own thing on the side. I'd help Dad sell the firm or turn it into a smaller specialist business well before 2039. I'd put money into a pension and an index fund. And I'd keep coaching the kids, because that's something that gives me energy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit eager. A decade feels like a good run-up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the church football club?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep coaching. If the world gets strange, kids still need someone to turn up on Sunday. It's the job I'd do for nothing, and I think that matters more as everything else gets automated.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still use the tools every day in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, of course. By then it'd be like electricity. The skill is knowing what to ask and when to say no.

say: Ten years is long, so **don't be afraid**; the young learn skills and the old share what they know.
At uni I'd say **build something** and don't wait to be asked.

My worry is my **dad**, whose trucking firm might not survive the robots in 2039.

Put money into a **pension** and an index fund.

S4.quote: If the world gets strange, kids still need someone to turn up on Sunday.
fieldNote: Keeps **coaching** as a human job he would do for nothing, and values it more as things automate.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Dad's firm would be hit right when I'm halfway through a degree, and there'd be no time to build anything before it lands. What would help is fast, practical support for small firms to adapt, training that people can actually use, and communities, like church, that keep people together. I'd not want handouts without a path to work, but I'd want a bridge.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd say we're not naive. We use the tools every day and we see the risks. I just think the answer is more building, more neighbours helping each other, and less waiting for someone to rescue us.

headlineQuote: I'd say we're not naive. We use the tools every day and we see the risks.
portrait: Liam is an **18-year-old** software engineering student who uses AI daily and sells refurbished phones for about 200 a month.
His dad runs an **eleven-truck** firm and his mum is a school secretary, so money and the drivers' jobs weigh on him.
He is **traditional** and entrepreneurial, favouring work, church and neighbours over handouts, and wanting to own something.
He is calm when things are slow and **alarmed at two years**, when he would put family and income before the degree.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** worries him most: his dad's firm hit mid-degree, with no time to build anything first.
whatWouldHelp: Fast, practical support for **small firms**, usable training, and communities like church that keep people together.
